title: Body and health
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 4.5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedTenses: present — including for a pain that started in the past and is still here

rules.text: THE BODY PART IS THE SUBJECT, SO THE VERB AGREES WITH IT. mi fa male la testa is literally "the head makes bad to me", and two feet make the verb plural: mi fanno male i piedi. L2-M8 shipped the singular and a learner who stops there will say mi fa male i piedi at the one moment it matters, because English "my feet hurt" gives no warning. It is the same backwards shape as mi piace and mi piacciono.

THE BODY PART TAKES A DEFINITE ARTICLE, NEVER A POSSESSIVE. mi fa male la testa, not mi fa male la mia testa. The mi has already said whose head it is, and saying it twice is the single loudest marker of a learner in a doctor's room. en-es states the same law with me duele la cabeza, and Arabic does the same work with its own suffix — one habit, three courses.

DA DOES BOTH "FOR" AND "SINCE", AND THE TENSE STAYS PRESENT. mi fa male da tre giorni ("for three days"), mi fa male da lunedì ("since Monday") — one Italian word for two English ones, and no perfect anywhere. English cannot say "it hurts for three days" and must reach for "it has been hurting"; Italian simply keeps the present, because the pain is still here.

SYMPTOMS ARE THINGS YOU HAVE, AND THEY KEEP THEIR ARTICLE: ho la febbre, ho la tosse, ho il raffreddore. Beside them sits the fixed frame mal di, which takes a bare body part with no article at all — mal di testa, mal di gola, mal di stomaco. That is the phrase a pharmacy is told, and the one worth learning whole.

words.note: The plural of L2-M8's mi fa male. Two feet make the verb plural, because the feet are the subject and you are only the mi.

sentences.trap: English "my feet hurt" puts the feet where a subject goes and Italian puts them last, which makes it easy to leave the verb singular. The verb counts the parts, not the person.
sentences.sound: mee FAN-no MA-le ee PYE-dee. fanno holds its double n, and the whole thing runs as one phrase.

variations.display: Mi fa male il piede
variations.cue: My foot hurts
variations.changed: one foot, so the verb goes singular

variations.display: Ti fanno male i piedi?
variations.cue: Do your feet hurt?
variations.changed: asked of somebody else

variations.display: Mi fanno male le gambe
variations.cue: My legs hurt
variations.changed: a different pair

mistake.why: Two feet, plural verb: Mi fanno male i piedi.

sentences.usage: Said after a long day, and said to a doctor exactly the same way.
sentences.mnemonic: Count the parts, not the people.

sentences.display: Mi fa male la gola da tre giorni
sentences.cue: My throat has been hurting for three days
sentences.literal: To-me it-makes bad the throat from three days

words.note: Feminine: la gola. It is the part that turns up most at a pharmacy counter, in the frame mal di gola.
One word for both English ones: da tre giorni is "for three days", da lunedì is "since Monday". The verb in front of it stays present.
Masculine, plural in -i. L1-M4's ogni giorno and tutti i giorni are built from the singular.

sentences.trap: English forces a perfect here — "has been hurting" — and Italian forbids one. Reaching for mi ha fatto male da tre giorni says the pain finished, which is the opposite of what you mean.
sentences.sound: mee fa MA-le la GO-la da tre JOR-nee. giorni starts with a soft j sound.

variations.display: Mi fa male la gola da lunedì
variations.cue: My throat has been hurting since Monday
variations.changed: a starting point instead of a length

variations.display: Mi fa male la testa da due giorni
variations.cue: My head has been hurting for two days
variations.changed: a different part and a different count

variations.display: Non mi fa male la gola
variations.cue: My throat does not hurt
variations.changed: negative, and no duration

mistake.display: Mi fa male la mia gola da tre giorni
mistake.why: The mi already says whose throat it is: Mi fa male la gola da tre giorni.

sentences.usage: The opening line at a pharmacy or a doctor's — the part, then how long.
sentences.mnemonic: da = for AND since, and the verb never moves.

sentences.display: Ho la febbre e la tosse
sentences.cue: I have a fever and a cough
sentences.literal: I-have the fever and the cough

words.note: Feminine, and it keeps its article: ho la febbre, where English says "a fever" or none at all.
Feminine, also with its article: ho la tosse. The double s is held.

sentences.trap: English drops the article — "I have fever" — and Italian keeps it. ho febbre is understood but marks you at once; the la is not optional.
sentences.sound: o la FEB-bre e la TOS-se. Both words hold a double consonant, which is what makes them sound Italian rather than English.

variations.display: Ho la tosse da una settimana
variations.cue: I have had a cough for a week
variations.changed: how long it has lasted

variations.display: Non ho la febbre
variations.cue: I do not have a fever
variations.changed: negative

variations.display: Mio figlio ha la febbre
variations.cue: My son has a fever
variations.changed: somebody else has it

mistake.why: A symptom is a noun you have, not something you are: Ho la febbre.

sentences.usage: What you say when you call in sick, in exactly this order.
sentences.mnemonic: You HAVE the fever, article and all.

sentences.cue: I have had a cold since Monday

words.note: Masculine: ho il raffreddore. Nothing to do with freddo the temperature, though the two words look related.

sentences.trap: da lunedì is "since Monday", and the Italian verb stays in the present. English cannot manage that and reaches for "have had", which tempts a learner into the passato prossimo.
sentences.sound: o eel raf-fred-DO-re da lu-ne-DEE. lunedì is stressed on the final ì, which is why it carries the accent.

variations.display: Ho il raffreddore da tre giorni
variations.cue: I have had a cold for three days
variations.changed: a length instead of a starting point

variations.display: Ho il raffreddore e mal di gola
variations.cue: I have a cold and a sore throat
variations.changed: a second symptom in the fixed frame

variations.display: Non ho il raffreddore, ho la tosse
variations.cue: I do not have a cold, I have a cough
variations.changed: correcting which symptom it is

mistake.display: Ho avuto il raffreddore da lunedì
mistake.why: The past says the cold is over. Still have it, so: Ho il raffreddore da lunedì.

sentences.usage: An explanation, not a complaint — the sentence that excuses a missed evening.

words.note: A fixed frame taking a bare body part with no article: mal di testa, mal di gola, mal di stomaco. It is L2-M8's male, shortened inside this phrase only.
Masculine, stressed on the STO. Both mal di stomaco and mi fa male lo stomaco are said.

sentences.trap: The article that is compulsory everywhere else is forbidden here: mal di gola, never mal di la gola. The frame swallows it.
sentences.sound: o mal dee STO-ma-ko. stomaco is stressed on the first syllable, not the second, which English speakers reliably get wrong.

variations.display: Ho mal di testa
variations.cue: I have a headache
variations.changed: a different part in the same frame

variations.display: Ho mal di gola da tre giorni
variations.cue: I have had a sore throat for three days
variations.changed: how long it has lasted

variations.display: Mi fa male lo stomaco
variations.cue: My stomach hurts
variations.changed: the long way round, with the article back

mistake.why: mal di takes the bare part: Ho mal di stomaco.

sentences.usage: The commonest complaint in the language, and short enough to say to a stranger.

sentences.display: Mi fa male la schiena da una settimana
sentences.cue: My back has been hurting for a week
sentences.literal: To-me it-makes bad the back from a week

words.note: Feminine: la schiena. The sch is a hard sk sound, as in schedule spoken the American way.
Feminine. L1-M6 shipped la settimana prossima whole; this is the bare noun inside it.

sentences.trap: One back, so the verb is singular here — but the moment the complaint becomes le gambe or i piedi the verb has to move to fanno, and nothing in the English sentence signals that.
sentences.sound: mee fa MA-le la SKYE-na da OO-na set-ti-MA-na. schiena begins sk, never sh.

variations.display: Mi fa male la schiena da ieri
variations.cue: My back has been hurting since yesterday
variations.changed: a starting point instead of a length

variations.display: Mi fanno male le gambe da una settimana
variations.cue: My legs have been hurting for a week
variations.changed: plural parts, so the verb goes plural

variations.display: Mi fa male la schiena quando lavoro
variations.cue: My back hurts when I work
variations.changed: when it hurts instead of how long

mistake.display: La mia schiena fa male da una settimana
mistake.why: Italian keeps you in the mi and the back in the article: Mi fa male la schiena da una settimana.

sentences.usage: The complaint of anybody who sits or lifts for a living — very common, and not dramatic.
sentences.mnemonic: One back, fa. Two legs, fanno.

sentences.display: Mi fa male il braccio, non la gamba
sentences.cue: My arm hurts, not my leg
sentences.literal: To-me it-makes bad the arm, not the leg

words.note: Masculine singular, but the plural le braccia is feminine — a small closed class of body parts does this. Learn the pair, not a rule.
Feminine and entirely ordinary: la gamba, le gambe. It is the plural you will say more often.

sentences.trap: English repeats "my" in the second half — "not my leg" — and Italian repeats only the article. Putting mia back in is the same doubling the module's second rule warns about.
sentences.sound: mee fa MA-le eel BRAT-cho, non la GAM-ba. The cci in braccio is a hard tch.

variations.display: Mi fanno male le braccia
variations.cue: My arms hurt
variations.changed: the feminine plural, and the verb with it

variations.display: Mi fa male la gamba da ieri
variations.cue: My leg has been hurting since yesterday
variations.changed: how long it has hurt

variations.display: Non mi fa male il braccio
variations.cue: My arm does not hurt
variations.changed: negative

mistake.why: The plural of this one is feminine: Mi fanno male le braccia.

sentences.usage: Correcting a doctor who has reached for the wrong limb — precise, and worth being precise about.
sentences.mnemonic: il braccio, le braccia — it changes sides in the plural.

sentences.display: Ha qualcosa per il mal di gola?
sentences.cue: Do you have something for a sore throat?
sentences.literal: You-have something for the bad of throat?

words.note: One word, never split. qualcosa di buono needs a di before an adjective, which is why it is worth its own row.

sentences.trap: The verb is ha, not hai — this is the polite address of a counter, the form L2-M1's scusi and senta belong to. Nothing about the sentence looks formal except that one letter.
sentences.sound: a kwal-KO-za per eel mal dee GO-la. The whole question rises only at the very end.

variations.display: Ha qualcosa per il mal di testa?
variations.cue: Do you have something for a headache?
variations.changed: a different complaint

variations.display: Ha qualcosa per la tosse?
variations.cue: Do you have something for a cough?
variations.changed: a symptom instead of an ache

variations.display: Scusi, ha qualcosa per la febbre?
variations.cue: Excuse me, do you have something for a fever?
variations.changed: opened with L2-M1's scusi

mistake.display: Hai qualcosa per il mal di gola?
mistake.why: A pharmacist is addressed politely, so the verb is third person: Ha qualcosa per il mal di gola?

sentences.usage: The whole pharmacy transaction in one line. Say it, and you will be handed something.
sentences.mnemonic: ha, not hai — the counter takes the polite form.

sentences.display: Vado in farmacia e prendo una pastiglia
sentences.cue: I am going to the pharmacy and taking a tablet
sentences.literal: I-go in pharmacy and I-take a tablet

words.note: Feminine, stressed on the CI: far-ma-CHEE-a. in farmacia takes no article, like in ufficio.
Feminine. The word on the box; compressa is what the box itself often prints.

sentences.trap: in farmacia has no article where English has "the". Italian drops it for places you go to for their purpose, exactly as L3-M2 does with in ufficio.
sentences.sound: VA-do een far-ma-CHEE-a e PREN-do OO-na pas-TEE-lya. The gli in pastiglia is the soft sound from voglia.

variations.display: Vado in farmacia adesso
variations.cue: I am going to the pharmacy now
variations.changed: when, using M6's adesso

variations.display: Prendo una pastiglia per il mal di testa
variations.cue: I take a tablet for a headache
variations.changed: what the tablet is for

variations.display: Il medico ha detto di prendere una pastiglia
variations.cue: The doctor said to take a tablet
variations.changed: reported as an instruction, with L3-M5's di

mistake.why: in farmacia carries no article: Vado in farmacia.

sentences.usage: The ordinary next step after the pharmacy question, and how you would tell a friend what you are doing.
sentences.mnemonic: in farmacia, in ufficio — no article for the places you go for a reason.

sentences.display: Da quando hai mal di gola?
sentences.cue: How long have you had a sore throat?
sentences.literal: From when you-have bad of throat?

words.note: The question this module's da answers. Italian asks it in the present, where English must reach for "have you had".

sentences.trap: The English question is in a perfect and the Italian one is not. Da quando hai avuto asks when a finished illness happened, which is a different question altogether.
sentences.sound: da KWAN-do eye mal dee GO-la. hai is one syllable, rhyming with English "eye".

variations.display: Da quando ti fa male la testa?
variations.cue: How long has your head been hurting?
variations.changed: the long frame instead of mal di

variations.display: Da quando hai la febbre?
variations.cue: How long have you had a fever?
variations.changed: a symptom instead of an ache

variations.display: Da quando ti fanno male i piedi?
variations.cue: How long have your feet been hurting?
variations.changed: plural parts, so the verb goes plural

mistake.display: Da quando hai avuto mal di gola?
mistake.why: The past asks about a sore throat that is over: Da quando hai mal di gola?

sentences.usage: What a doctor asks first, and what you should expect to be asked.
sentences.mnemonic: da quando + present = how long so far.
